passage:
Rain hammered the windows, so recess was indoors. When the teacher's red marker went missing, thirty heads turned to Devika before anyone said a word.

“It's always her,” a boy muttered. Devika shrugged. “Fine. I took it.” Her voice was flat, as if she'd said it many times. She hadn't taken it.

Yash stared at his desk. The marker lay under his geometry box, and his ears burned. He said nothing.

The teacher looked from Devika's face to the class. “Devika, stay a moment.” In the empty room she asked, “Did you really take it?” Devika looked at the floor. “Does it matter? Everyone thinks so.”

The teacher crouched to her level and said, “It matters to me.”

qa.q: Where was the red marker really hidden?
qa.a: The red marker lay under Yash's geometry box.

qa.q: Why did Devika say, “Fine. I took it,” when she had not taken it?
qa.a: Devika felt resigned and hopeless after being blamed so many times, so saying yes felt easier than arguing again.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Devika differently from the class?
qa.a: The teacher asked Devika to stay back, asked calmly if Devika really took it, and said it mattered to the teacher.

qa.q: What might Yash be feeling, staring at the desk while the marker lay under the geometry box?
qa.a: Yash is probably scared and guilty, fearing trouble yet ashamed to see Devika blamed, and cannot find the courage to speak.

grounding: A child who is always blamed expects it and admits a theft she did not commit, while a real culprit stays silent and a teacher asks calmly.

passage:
Ammi's voice came from the sitting room. “Who spilled juice on the sofa? Farida!”

Farida did not answer or argue. She walked to the kitchen for the cloth, shoulders low, like she'd done a hundred times. Her little brother Zaid, six, slid his glass behind a cushion. Irawati, a classmate who had come over to study, had seen everything, and she gripped her pencil.

“Sorry, Ammi,” Farida said, dabbing at the stain. “I'm the messy one, I know.”

Irawati's voice came out small. “It wasn't Farida.”

Ammi paused, cloth in hand. She looked at Zaid's cushion, then at her daughter kneeling on the floor, and slowly put her hand on Farida's back.

qa.q: Who spilled the juice on the sofa?
qa.a: Zaid spilled the juice; the glass was hidden behind a cushion.

qa.q: Why did Farida say “I'm the messy one, I know” without arguing?
qa.a: Farida feels defeated and ashamed after being blamed so often; Farida has started to see the label as true and no longer expects to be believed.

qa.q: What choice did Irawati make, and what did it change?
qa.a: Irawati spoke up quietly that it was not Farida, and that made Ammi stop, look at Zaid and comfort Farida.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel after looking at Zaid's cushion and then at Farida on the floor?
qa.a: Ammi may feel surprised and sorry at how quickly the blame fell on Farida, and realise how long the label has been sticking.

grounding: A child who is habitually blamed at home takes the label as her self-image until a visiting classmate speaks up.

passage:
Monday
Someone's eraser went missing again. Before anyone even looked, Rinku said, “Chandrika must have it.” Ms Joseph looked at me. I didn't even argue this time.
At home it's the same. Francis breaks the remote, and Mummy says, “Chandrika, why did you let him?” If milk spills, it's me.
I used to cry about it. Now I just shrug. It's like watching a film about someone else. Today I thought, fine, if I'm the bad one, I'll be the bad one. I didn't do my homework on purpose.
Ms Joseph found the eraser under Rinku's bag at the end of the day. She said sorry to me. I said okay. I didn't feel anything.

qa.q: Where was the eraser found?
qa.a: It was found under Rinku's bag.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's "I didn't feel anything" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Chandrika has grown numb and detached from being blamed all the time, a way to stop hurting.

qa.q: How could Ms Joseph help Chandrika beyond saying sorry?
qa.a: She could check facts before looking at Chandrika, praise Chandrika openly for small things, and talk with the family about the pattern.

qa.q: How might Francis see things at home?
qa.a: He may not realise the unfairness, since he gets away with breaking things while Chandrika takes the blame.

grounding: A child writes about being the default culprit at school and home, becoming detached and taking on the label of the bad one.

passage:
In their village near Bhandara, whenever a window broke or a hen went missing, the answer came quickly: “Manoj.”
His cousin Gautam could steal mangoes from the schoolmaster's tree and still be called a good boy. Manoj could be sitting at home and still be blamed.
At first Manoj argued. Then he stopped. Now, when the older boys threw stones at the water tank, he threw one too, hard, straight at it. “They'll say it was me anyway,” he muttered.
Gautam stared at him. “You're making it worse.”
Manoj shrugged. His eyes looked flat, like nothing mattered.
Their grandfather, watching from the verandah, called Manoj over, and for the first time asked, “Tell me what happened, beta,” before deciding anything.

qa.q: Whose tree did Gautam steal mangoes from?
qa.a: He stole mangoes from the schoolmaster's tree.

qa.q: What does Manoj's flat look suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels hopeless and detached, as if being blamed so often has made him stop caring.

qa.q: What did the grandfather do that could help Manoj?
qa.a: He asked Manoj what happened before deciding, which gives him a fair hearing instead of automatic blame.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel watching Manoj throw the stone?
qa.a: He seems surprised and worried, maybe starting to see how unfair the blame has been.

grounding: Shows a village boy who is always blamed and begins to act out, taking on the label because he'll be blamed anyway.

passage:
In their school in Prague, Jana had become the one Mr Novák looked at first. Talking in class? “Jana.” Paint on the floor? “Jana.” Even when she was absent once, he said, “This mess, was it Jana yesterday?”
She stopped raising her hand. At break she sat alone on the stairs, drawing in her notebook margin.
Her friend Nadia sat beside her. “You didn't do the paint thing. I saw Petr.”
“Doesn't matter,” Jana said. “I'm the problem kid. That's just what I am.”
Nadia frowned. “That's not true.”
Jana shrugged and kept drawing. That afternoon, Nadia went to the class teacher and told her what she had seen. The class teacher thanked her and asked Jana to stay after school for a kind talk over cocoa.

qa.q: What did Jana draw in?
qa.a: She drew in her notebook margin.

qa.q: How does Jana feel when she says "I'm the problem kid"?
qa.a: She feels hopeless and detached, having come to believe the label, so she no longer even defends herself.

qa.q: What did Nadia do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She told the class teacher what she saw that afternoon, which got an adult to listen to Jana kindly.

qa.q: How might Nadia feel seeing Jana accept the label?
qa.a: Nadia probably feels sad and frustrated, knowing a friend is being unfairly blamed.

grounding: Shows a child who becomes the default culprit in class and starts to take on the label, withdrawing, until a friend tells a teacher.

passage:
At the after-school tuition centre, the whiteboard marker went missing again. Before anyone spoke, Gurleen said, "I didn't take it," and folded her arms. Nobody had asked her.
Hansa didi, the tutor, glanced at her. So did the four others at the table. Gurleen's jaw set. Last week it was the missing sharpener, the week before, the spilled water. Always, "Gurleen, again?"
"Whatever," she muttered. "I'm the bad one anyway." She kicked the table leg, just hard enough to make the pencils jump.
Then Hansa didi found the marker in her own bag. She came and sat beside Gurleen. "It was with me. I'm sorry you had to defend yourself before anyone asked. You're not the bad one."

qa.q: Where did Hansa didi find the marker?
qa.a: In her own bag.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen say "I didn't take it" before anyone asked?
qa.a: Gurleen expected to be blamed as usual, so she felt defensive and hurt even before anyone spoke.

qa.q: What could Hansa didi do next to help Gurleen drop the "bad one" label?
qa.a: Ask what actually happened before looking at anyone, and notice Gurleen's good moments out loud, so the old label stops sticking.

qa.q: How might Hansa didi feel on finding the marker in her own bag?
qa.a: Hansa didi likely felt sorry and a little ashamed, seeing how quickly everyone, including her, had looked at Gurleen.

grounding: Shows a child who has become the default culprit, expects blame and starts to take on the label of the bad one.
